name: Imre Halász
equipment: Heavy coat: a black wool coat he brought from Hungary in 1904, patched with miners' canvas
Walking stick, an ash stick with a brass ferrule he turned himself
The Kept Light: a brass Wolf flame safety lamp, the oldest in Ottway, which he trimmed, filled and kept burning under the check board from 15 October 1919 to 1 March 1927; it is cold now
Nine brass checks on a loop of wire, picked out of the slate dump on the night of 1 March: Nos. 112, 118, 156, 203, 207, 219, 241, 266 and 288
A tenth check, cut from a blank and stamped by hand with the letters E P and no number
A lamp man's tool roll: wick picks, a gauze brush, a spanner for the bonnet, spare glasses and gauzes, a can of naphtha
A rosary he does not use and does not put away
His dismissal slip, dated 1 March 1927: 'Services no longer required. Company house to be vacated by 1 May.'
features: Something to Hold On To (Faithful origin: once per long rest, when he would gain Dread, he gains 1 fewer; advantage on saves against being charmed or compelled; no miracle in it)

Old Lore (Occultist: once the party has seen a creature or clear sign of it, an action and an INT (Occult) check, DC 10 + its CR, recalls one of its rules the party has not yet learned, which the GM chooses and which is always true; once per creature per long rest. Advantage on Occult checks to perform a rite or set a ward, in half the time)

The Right Things in the Bag (Occultist: once per scenario, when a rite or ward needs a common object he could plausibly carry, a wick, a lamp glass, a brass check blank, chalk, a little naphtha, he has it)
Steeped in It (Occultist, 2nd level: advantage on fear checks against the sign of a horror, DC 10; whenever he or the party learn one of a creature's rules, he loses 1 Dread)
Tradition: Collector (Occultist, 3rd level: his curio is the Kept Light, the Wolf lamp; once per scenario its history gives a clue the GM chooses, usually about what light does to the thing below)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: he can strip, repair and test any mine lamp, flame or electric, and most other machines; a few minutes with one tells him what is wrong with it, including whether someone made it go wrong)
traits: The Right Things in the Bag

personality.traits: I am slow, and exact, and I hum while I work. I call every miner by his check number and his name, both, every time. I apologise for my English, which is better than most people's.
personality.ideals: A lamp man's whole work is to know who is underground. Every man who takes a lamp from me, I count him down and I count him up. Fourteen I never counted up. Until they come up, they are still mine to count.
personality.bonds: The fourteen, especially my cousin József Kertész, No. 207, and Ezell Pettaway, who had no number, so I gave him one. The Kept Light. Lettie Burchett, who brings me soup and pretends she was passing.
personality.flaws: I never asked why I kept the light. I only knew I had to. I told nobody, because a lamp man who says the dead need a light is a lamp man who is laughed at, and then on the first of March I let a young man with a badge put it out with his thumb, and I did not stop him.

appearance: A thin, stooped, white-moustached man of sixty-three with a bald freckled head, very clear blue eyes behind steel spectacles, and long clever fingers stained with naphtha. A black coat, a collarless shirt, a lamp man's leather apron he still wears from habit, and the cold brass lamp, which he carries everywhere in a canvas bag.
backstory: Imre Halász came from a village in the hills of northern Hungary in 1904 to the anthracite mines of Pennsylvania, and from there to Ottway in 1911, where his knees gave out underground and the company made him lamp man. For sixteen years he ran the lamp house at the drift mouth: every man who went into No. 3 hung one brass check on the board and took a lamp, and Imre counted them down and counted them up. On 14 October 1919, thirteen checks stayed on the board, and Imre stamped a fourteenth from a blank for Ezell Pettaway, whom he had known, and who had loaded on Moses Hairston's number and so did not exist to the company. On 15 October, when they sealed 7 North, he lit his oldest Wolf lamp and hung it under the fourteen checks, without quite knowing why, and he kept it burning, every shift, every Sunday, through the strike of 1922 and two winters of short time, for seven and a half years. Nobody asked; it was Imre's lamp house. On 1 March 1927 the company put in the new electric cap lamps, and the new Ironwood captain, Arliss Kincaid, came in to clear the old board and said there would be no open flame in the lamp house now. A young guard pinched out the Kept Light, the checks went into a bucket and the bucket onto the slate dump, and Imre was dismissed the same afternoon for having been seen at Mount Moriah on a Sunday night. He found nine checks on the dump by lantern light. The other four, and the board, he has not found. The first man went missing three weeks later.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Imre is the key to Rule 1 and Rule 5 (campaignRules: The Blackdamp's Rules), and he does not know it. He can tell the party what he did and when, in exact detail, but he has no theory: he kept a light for the men because the men were not counted up. Played straight he is the gentlest person in the campaign. With Old Lore he can, once the party has seen the Dark or its sign, recall a rule; on his first success give him Rule 2 (only the alone), from his own memory: 'In the old country they said: never let a man go down alone, because the dark is hungry. I thought it was about the roof.' He carries CLUE C1 (his account), C3 (the timing), D3 (Ezell's hand-cut check) and half of the material for the Kept Light rite: the lamp and ten checks. He will relight it at once if told how, and he must be the one to say József's name.
dmNotes.voice: Careful, slightly formal English with a Hungarian music to it, the articles sometimes missing. Calls men by number and name: 'Two-oh-seven, József.' Hums a Hungarian lullaby when trimming a wick. Never raises his voice.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: count the fourteen up, and see them buried. Secondary: get his lamp house back, or at least the board. Tertiary: not to be evicted on 1 May with nowhere to go.
dmNotes.secrets: He saw, on the night of 1 March, walking home past the drift mouth with his bucket of checks, the lamps of the night shift going blue one after another down the main heading, as far as he could see, and then coming back, and he went home and sat up all night with the cold lamp on his knees. He also knows that Superintendent Bledsoe came to the lamp house on 23 October 1919, late, alone, stood in front of the board for a long time, and said 'It's quit, Imre. They've quit knocking.' He has never repeated it.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: grateful for any kindness, guarded about the lamp until someone takes it seriously. Toward Morris Pettaway: the warmest regard; he has kept Ezell's check for eight years and will give it to Morris with both hands. Toward Captain Kincaid: no anger, only fear. Toward Bledsoe: pity, which he would be ashamed to say aloud.
